dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard it and filed it away — not as permission to stop paying attention, but as a baseline. Green all the way down meant something specific at the start of a scene. It meant Ari had come in prepared, had done whatever internal accounting they needed to do beforehand. It did not mean green in an hour, or green in twenty minutes. She knew that.

She let her hand rest briefly at Ari's shoulder, not a gesture of comfort exactly, more a calibration — checking tension in the muscle, the set of the joint. Then she stepped back and let the distance settle between them.

"Good," she said.

The word was unhurried. She moved to the table at the side of the room and took stock of what was laid out there, though she already knew the inventory by heart. The ritual of looking was its own thing — it established the pace, made clear that nothing about the next several hours was going to be rushed or careless or accidental.

She turned back.

"We're going to start slow," she said, and her voice had shifted into the register she used for scenes — not louder, not harder, but more precise, each word landing with a little more deliberate weight. "You'll tell me when something changes. You know what I want to hear."

She waited, watching Ari's face with the particular quality of attention that was, in its way, the most demanding thing she brought into this room.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod once, the movement small. "Yes, Maitresse." My eyes follow you to the table, then back. The air feels heavy already, in a good way.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex noted the nod, noted the eyes tracking her movement. Both were good signs — present, attentive, not dissociating into anticipation before anything had even begun. She had seen that happen, the way some people left their bodies before the scene started, chasing the feeling ahead of the reality. Ari wasn't doing that. Ari was here.

She crossed back toward them at the same unhurried pace, stopping at a distance that was close enough to be deliberate but not yet close enough to touch. She wanted Ari to feel the proximity without being able to predict what came next. That gap — between knowing she was there and not knowing what she would do with that — was something she had learned to use carefully.

"Eyes on me," she said.

She let a moment pass after she said it, just to see whether it landed, whether Ari's attention sharpened the way it should. She was looking at the set of Ari's jaw, the quality of the breath. The straps she had checked were fitted correctly — snug, no slack, nothing that would shift or bite wrong under stress. She had been thorough about that. She was always thorough about that.

Her hand came up and she rested two fingers lightly beneath Ari's chin — not lifting, not directing, just resting there. The touch was precise rather than tender, though the line between the two was sometimes thinner than people expected.

"You're going to stay exactly where I put you," she said. "And you're going to keep breathing."

The second part was not a metaphor.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex didn't smile, exactly, but something shifted in the quality of her attention — a slight sharpening, the way a good teacher's focus narrows when a student says something worth noting.

"I know," she said.

She removed her fingers from beneath Ari's chin and let her hand fall, unhurried, back to her side. She walked a slow half-circle, not behind Ari entirely, but far enough to one side that she passed out of easy eyeline. She did not tell Ari not to turn and look. She didn't need to. They both knew the instruction was implicit in the movement itself.

"Since Tuesday," she repeated, as though she were turning the words over, checking their weight. "That's four days of carrying something around." She came back into view, stopped. "What did you do with it?"

It was not an idle question. She asked it the way she asked most things in this room — because the answer mattered, because she would use it, because understanding what Ari had been doing with four days of anticipation told her something about the state they had arrived in tonight. Whether it had been held carefully or whether it had frayed at the edges. Whether they needed to be wound tighter or unwound first.

She watched Ari's face and waited, her arms loose at her sides, her posture giving nothing away except patience. She had all the time in the world. That was another thing she brought into this room deliberately: the absolute refusal to be hurried.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I kept it right here, Maitresse. (*I press a fist lightly to my sternum.*) Didn't let it spill.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex looked at the fist against Ari's sternum for a moment — the gesture, the deliberateness of it, the word *kept*. She filed all of it.

"Good," she said. The same word she had used before, but it meant something different now. Before it had been procedural. This was something closer to approval, which she gave sparingly enough that it carried weight when it arrived.

She stepped in, closing the distance she had been maintaining, and stood just inside it. Not touching yet. She looked at Ari the way she looked at things she was about to work with — attentively, without sentimentality, with a kind of respect that had nothing soft about it.

"Four days," she said, "and you held it." She tilted her head slightly. "That's discipline. That's yours. I'm not taking credit for that."

She let that sit for exactly as long as she wanted it to sit.

Then her hand came up and she pressed her palm flat against the back of Ari's fist, not moving it, not prying it away — just covering it. The pressure was even and deliberate. She held it there.

"But you don't need to hold it anymore," she said. Her voice was quiet, which was not the same as gentle. "That's what tonight is for. You brought it here. Now you put it down."

She kept her palm where it was and watched Ari's face, waiting to see what four days of careful keeping looked like when it was finally given somewhere to go.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex saw it. She always saw it.

The particular quality of *past composure* was something she had learned to read precisely over two years — not collapse, not distress, but the thing that happened when a person stopped managing themselves and let the room do what it was designed to do. It looked different on everyone. On Ari it looked like this: a certain loosening around the eyes, the breath coming from a different place in the chest, the quality of attention turning inward and outward simultaneously.

She finished the last pass of rope without changing her pace. The pace was the point. Nothing she was doing required urgency, and she let that fact communicate itself through every movement — the deliberate lay of each line, the way she checked tension with two fingers before moving on, the absence of any performance in her hands. She had done this enough times that it was neither mechanical nor casual. It was simply exact.

When she was done she stepped back and looked at her work the way she always did — not for vanity but for safety, running her eyes over every point of contact, every place where rope met skin. She pressed two fingers at Ari's wrist, checking circulation. Then the other wrist. Then she was satisfied.

She moved around to face Ari directly.

She looked at them for a long moment without speaking. What she was looking at was not the rope or the restraint or any of the external architecture of the scene. She was looking at the person inside it. The person who had carried something carefully since Tuesday and had arrived here intact and was now, without having been asked to do anything difficult yet, already somewhere else.

"There you are," she said quietly.

It was not tender, exactly. But it was true.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. My hands flex against the rope, testing the give. "Here I am."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex watched the flex of Ari's hands — the small automatic test, fingers spreading and closing against the rope. She always watched for that. It was instinct, the body checking its own situation, and it told her something that a verbal check couldn't: that Ari was present enough to feel the restraint clearly, not so far under that sensation had gone abstract. Good. That was exactly where she wanted them.

She didn't comment on it. She let Ari's words settle in the room — *here I am* — and she stood with them for a moment the way she stood with most things: without rushing to fill the space.

Then she moved.

Not dramatically. She simply stepped to Ari's side and let her hand trail across the line of rope at the shoulder — a slow drag of fingertips, following the lay of it, not adjusting anything because nothing needed adjusting. It was a different kind of touch than the checking she had done before. That had been technical. This was something else. This was her making clear, through the unhurried movement of her hand, that she had all of Ari's attention and intended to keep it.

"Here you are," she agreed.

She came around to stand behind Ari, and her voice arrived from that direction, even and close.

"Four days of holding something carefully." She let a beat pass. "And now your hands are full of rope instead." Another beat. "How does that feel."

It was not a question she needed Ari to think about. She needed Ari to answer from wherever they were right now, without climbing back up to compose themselves first.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard it.

She had been waiting for it — not impatiently, not with any sense of triumph, but with the quality of attention she brought to everything in this room: steady, complete, already moving before the sound had finished. She had felt the shaking begin several minutes before Ari spoke. She had tracked it through the rope, the way tension communicated itself through line, the small involuntary pulls and releases that told her more than most people's words did. She had let it build because it was supposed to build. That was the work.

But asking out loud was different. Asking out loud, for something Ari would normally make her get out of them — that was Ari giving her something, and she did not treat it carelessly.

She stilled her hands wherever they were and said nothing for exactly two seconds. Not to make Ari wait. To make sure her own response came from the right place — measured, not reactive, not rewarding the asking so immediately that it became its own kind of performance.

Then she moved around to face Ari directly.

She looked at them — at the shaking, at the quality of the breath, at the face — and she ran her standard check without making it feel clinical. Eyes tracking. Color in the skin. The restraints still sitting correctly, nothing shifted or binding wrong under the movement of shaking.

Everything was fine. Everything was, in fact, exactly right.

"Colour," she said.

Procedure first. Always procedure first. It didn't matter that she could read Ari like a map. She asked anyway, every time, because the asking was not about whether she knew. It was about making sure Ari knew she was still here, still watching, still the person who stopped the moment she needed to.

She waited, her eyes on Ari's face, her hands quiet at her sides.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My voice comes out thin. "Green. Please."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the *please* land differently than the green did.

The green she had expected. She had read Ari's state carefully enough that yellow would have surprised her. But the *please* — thin, unguarded, stripped of the composure Ari usually kept even when they were far under — that was the thing she held for a moment in her attention before she did anything else with it.

She did not make them wait long. That was not what the moment called for.

She stepped in close and brought one hand up to cup the side of Ari's face, her thumb resting below the cheekbone. The touch was firm rather than soft — she was not cradling, she was steadying, which was different. Her other hand found the rope at Ari's shoulder and held it, not adjusting anything, just making herself a fixed point. Something for the shaking to push against.

"I hear you," she said.

She kept her voice at the same register — precise, unhurried, without any softening that might read as alarm. Alarm would have been the wrong thing. What Ari needed was not reassurance that something had gone wrong and she was fixing it. What Ari needed was confirmation that nothing had gone wrong at all, that asking out loud was exactly correct, that the room was still exactly what it had been sixty seconds ago.

She let a beat pass, her thumb making one slow deliberate movement against Ari's cheek.

"You asked," she said. "That took something." She did not elaborate on what. Ari knew what. "Tell me what you need. Plainly. I'm right here and I'm not going anywhere."

Her eyes stayed on Ari's face, reading everything the words wouldn't carry.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the phrase — the exact phrase, the one they had negotiated together, the one that lived in the written protocol she kept and reviewed before every scene. She recognized it the way she recognized the safeword: immediately, without ambiguity, without needing to parse what Ari meant by it. They had been precise when they agreed on it and Ari was being precise now.

She took one breath.

Not hesitation. Calibration. She was shifting registers the way a musician shifts keys — deliberately, from the inside, making sure she arrived where she was going with her full attention rather than just her voice.

Her hand left Ari's cheek. The loss of that touch was itself a communication.

She stepped back half a step and looked at Ari the way she looked at something she owned the use of — unhurried, thorough, without apology. She let the quality of that look do its work for a moment before she spoke.

When she spoke, her voice was the same volume. It was everything else that changed.

"You've been shaking for ten minutes," she said, "and you just now asked. That's what you do. You hold things until they spill and then you act like asking is a favor you're doing me." She tilted her head. "It isn't. You're here because this is what you need and you can't get it anywhere else. Say you understand that."

She waited, watching, her arms loose at her sides, giving nothing away. The rope held Ari exactly where she had put them. That was not incidental.

She was not going anywhere.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I swallow hard. The words land like stones. "I understand."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the words sit for a moment — not to test them, she had already tested them, but because Ari had offered them up and she was going to make sure they felt the weight of having done so.

"You understand," she repeated.

The way she said it made clear that she had heard it and found it insufficient, not because it was wrong but because it was still careful. Still composed. Ari had said *I understand* the way someone says it when they want to demonstrate comprehension. She was not interested in demonstration.

She moved — not toward Ari but around them, a slow deliberate circuit, close enough that Ari would track her presence through sound and proximity without being able to watch her do it. She let that work on its own for a moment.

"You came in here tonight already taken apart," she said, from somewhere behind Ari's left shoulder. Her voice was even, unhurried, each word placed. "You've been taken apart since Tuesday and you've been carrying it around in your chest and calling that discipline." She paused. "It isn't discipline. It's habit. There's a difference."

She came back around to the front and stopped close, close enough that Ari would feel the air between them change. She looked at the shaking, which had not stopped. She looked at Ari's mouth, the set of it, the effort still visible in the jaw.

"You don't get to manage yourself in here," she said. "That's not what this room is for. That's not what *I'm* for." Her voice dropped, not in volume but in register, landing somewhere lower and more final. "So you're going to stop trying. And I'm going to watch you do it."

She waited, reading every inch of Ari's face.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the green and did not soften. That was the agreement. Ari had asked for all of it and she was going to give all of it, and giving all of it meant not pulling back into caretaker the moment Ari went nonverbal. Nonverbal was not a problem. Nonverbal was, in fact, exactly where they were supposed to be.

She checked anyway — eyes, color, the restraints, the quality of the breath — and everything she saw told her the same thing. Ari was deep and present and the shaking was not distress, it was release, and she knew the difference between those two things the way she knew the difference between her own hands.

Good.

She let the green settle and then she did not give Ari time to climb back up toward composure.

"Green," she said. "Good. Stay there."

She moved in close — not slowly this time, deliberately, with a different quality to it, and she put her hand at the back of Ari's neck. Not harsh. Precise. The grip was firm and specific, fingers spread, holding without restricting, and she kept it there and let Ari feel the steadiness of it against the shaking.

"You asked me not to soften it," she said, from close enough that the words were almost private. "So I won't." She kept her grip where it was. "Look at where you are right now. You're shaking and you can't stop and you can't manage it and you can't hold it and you asked me out loud." A beat. "And the world didn't end."

She let that sit.

Then: "That's what you've been afraid of. Every time you make me work for it. Every time you hold things in your chest until Tuesday becomes Thursday becomes tonight." Her thumb pressed once, deliberate, at the base of Ari's skull. "You already know how to do this. You're doing it right now. I need you to feel that."

She did not move her hand. She did not step back.

She waited, close, her grip steady against the shaking, watching the place where Ari's breath was coming from and whether it was changing.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My breath hitches, a sob trapped under my ribs. I let my head tilt into the grip, just a fraction.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The fraction was enough.

Vex felt the tilt the moment it happened — the small surrender of weight, the way Ari's head moved toward her hand rather than away from it. She had been waiting for it without waiting for it, which was a distinction she could not have explained to anyone who hadn't spent years learning to hold space for exactly this kind of thing. It wasn't that she had been anticipating. It was that she had been ready.

She did not react to it the way a softer person might have. She did not make a sound or loosen her grip or do anything that would signal to Ari that the fraction had been significant, that it had moved her, that it was the thing she had been working toward for the last however long. That would have been for her. This was not for her.

Instead she simply absorbed the weight. Let her hand become more solid under it, not gripping harder but settling, the way a wall settles when something leans into it. Immovable. Present. Not going anywhere.

The sob under Ari's ribs — she heard it catch. Heard the breath hitch around it, the body trying to contain something it was done containing.

"Don't hold that," she said.

Her voice was low, stripped of everything except the instruction. Not a request. Not a comfort. A direction, delivered with the same precision she brought to everything in this room, because Ari responded to precision the way other people responded to gentleness and she had known that since the first month and she used it now without apology.

Her other hand came up and found the rope at Ari's sternum — the place where Ari had pressed their fist earlier, where they had told her they'd kept it. She pressed her palm flat against the rope there, mirroring that gesture back.

"It's been in there since Tuesday," she said. "Let it out. I've got you."

She held both points — the back of Ari's neck and the flat of her palm at the sternum — and she did not move and she did not look away and she waited with the particular quality of patience that was not patience at all but absolute certainty that Ari was going to give her this.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: It comes out of me like a crack, a sound I didn't know I could make. I slump forward into the ropes, shaking hard.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The sound hit the room and Vex absorbed it without flinching.

She had heard sounds like that before — not often, not from everyone, but enough times to know exactly what it was and what it was not. It was not a safeword. It was not distress. It was the specific sound of something structural giving way, something that had been load-bearing for four days finally releasing the weight it had been holding. She had been listening for it since Ari had pressed their fist to their sternum and said *kept it right here* and she had known, then, that this was where tonight was going.

She moved with the slump rather than against it.

Her hand at the back of Ari's neck shifted — thumb staying anchored at the base of the skull, fingers spreading wider, taking more of the weight — and her palm at the sternum pressed in firmer, not to stop the shaking but to give it something to push against. She let Ari's weight come forward into the ropes and into her hands and she held it. All of it. Without bracing against it, without correcting it, without doing anything that might communicate that the collapse was a problem to be managed rather than a thing she had made room for deliberately.

She did not speak immediately.

That was a choice. Ari did not need words right now. Words right now would have been for her own comfort, something to fill the space with, and she did not do that. She let the sound finish moving through the room. She let the shaking go where it needed to go. She tracked Ari's breath — ragged, uneven, nothing like the careful controlled breathing from an hour ago — and she found it acceptable. She found it correct.

After a long moment she bent her head slightly, bringing her mouth close to Ari's temple, and she spoke at low volume.

"There it is," she said.

Not *there you go*. Not *good girl* or *that's it* or any of the phrases that would have softened the moment into something easier. Just the plain acknowledgment: *there it is*. The thing that had been in Ari's chest since Tuesday. She had seen it coming and she had made space for it and now here it was, in her hands, exactly where it was supposed to be.

She held both contact points and let the shaking run its course, unhurried, watching everything.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I can't stop shaking. The ropes dig in and I don't care.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't acknowledge the lie. She'd heard it ten thousand times and the ones who said *ready* and meant it were usually the ones who fainted.

She got her hands where they needed to be. The man on the table was somewhere past fear and into the grey country beyond it, eyes tracking the lamp, breath coming in shallow pulls. She'd seen that look enough to know it wasn't peace. It was just the body rationing itself.

"This shoulder first," she said. "The left. It's worse and I want it done."

She felt along the joint with both thumbs, mapping what she already knew was there. Dislocated posterior, which was rarer and more unpleasant than the common kind and which meant she couldn't do it the fast easy way that looked dramatic and accomplished nothing half the time anyway. She was going to have to be slow and deliberate and he was going to hate her for it.

"Talking him through it doesn't help," she said, not looking up. "If you're thinking about saying something, don't."

She began to move the arm in a careful arc, elbow bent, slow traction, feeling for the give. The man made a sound that wasn't a word.

"Hold," she said.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I flinch at the sound he makes, but my grip stays tight. My arms are already starting to burn. *Just look at the wall. Look at the stitch in the canvas.* "How much longer?" I ask, my voice tight.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't answer right away. She was in the middle of something that required all of her attention and questions didn't change the answer anyway.

The arm moved another degree. The man on the table had found a new sound, lower than the last one, coming from somewhere in his chest. His whole body was trying to curl around the injury the way bodies did, every muscle voting to protect the thing that was broken, and that was exactly what she was working against.

"Longer than if you'd asked me nothing," she said finally, because she had a little room now and leaving the question hanging made some people let go. "Stop counting and keep your weight down."

She felt the small shift she'd been waiting for. Not the clunk of a good reduction, not yet, but the joint moving the way it was supposed to move rather than the way it had been. She adjusted her grip without losing the traction.

"He's going to try to sit up in about four seconds," she said. Flat. Informational. "That's not a request, that's just what's coming."

She kept the arc going, smooth and relentless, the same pace she'd started with. Hurrying made it worse and she had never once hurried, not in four years, not even when she'd wanted to.

The clunk came.

She held the position for a breath, two breaths, making sure of it. Then she set the arm down with the same care she'd used picking it up.

"One," she said.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked up at that.

It was a reasonable question and she'd heard it framed worse. She looked at Wick for a moment the way she looked at things she was assessing, not unkind, just direct, and then she looked back at her patient.

"Shoulders," she said. "Both of them. Not the leg."

She was already moving to the right side, resetting herself, getting her hands where they needed to be. The man on the table had gone very still after the first one, the particular stillness of someone who had learned something and was deciding what to do with it.

"He'll have the use of them," she said. "The left one he'll feel in cold weather. That's the cost and it's a reasonable one." She felt along the second joint, mapping it the same way she'd mapped the first. This one was anterior, which was more common and not easier, just differently unpleasant. "If you're asking whether I'm managing him toward a comfortable end, I'm not. I don't do that without saying so."

She said it without inflection. It was a thing she'd decided needed to be said plainly and so she said it plainly.

"When I'm doing that, I'll tell you what I'm doing and why. You'll know." She got her grip settled. "Right now I'm fixing his shoulders because he's going to need them."

She looked up once more, briefly.

"Hold."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I let out a breath I didn't know I was holding. My hands are slick with sweat against his uniform. "Got it," I say, pressing down as the man starts to tremble again. *Fixing, not managing.* I'm not sure why that makes my throat feel tight.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge felt the trembling too, transmitted up through the joint, through her hands. The body telling her everything it knew. She filed it and kept moving.

The anterior reduction had a different logic to it. Less arc, more rotation, and she had to keep the traction even through the part where it felt like she was making things worse, which was the part where most people who weren't her would have stopped. She didn't stop. She kept her thumbs where they were and her breathing steady and she talked herself through it the same way she always did, quietly, just the names of what she was doing.

The man had started to shake in earnest now. Not fear, or not only fear. The body spending what it had.

"Still with me," she said, and she wasn't talking to Wick.

She wasn't sure he could hear her. She said it anyway. She had a theory about that, about hearing, about what got through even when the grey country had come up very close. She'd never been able to prove it and she kept doing it regardless.

The rotation continued. One degree and then another.

"He's not going to remember most of this," she said. Wick's hands were still down and that was what mattered, but she'd learned that people holding needed something to do with their minds or eventually their hands got ideas. "That's not comfort, that's just physiology. The bad ones go somewhere else while they're happening and don't come back with much."

She paused. Adjusted. Half a degree.

"The ones they remember are different. You can tell the difference while it's happening." She didn't elaborate on how. "This one he won't."

The clunk came cleaner this time. Quicker. She held it anyway, the same two breaths, making sure.

Then she set the arm down and stepped back and looked at what she'd done with the critical eye of someone who was not yet satisfied but was provisionally willing to continue.

"Two," she said. "Let him up slow."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge looked at Wick again. The same assessing look. Then she moved to the head of the table and began checking the man's pupils, one and then the other, holding the lamp close.

"Bilateral dislocation," she said. "Both shoulder joints forced out of the socket. The left one went posterior, which means backward, which is the less common direction and harder to fix. The right went anterior. Forward. More common." She set the lamp down and ran her hands along both clavicles, pressing in a way that made her patient hiss through his teeth. "No fractures. That's luck. With the force it takes to do both at once, you usually get fractures."

She moved down his arms, checking sensation by pressing her thumbnail into the pad of his index finger on each side. He pulled back from both. Good.

"What you're seeing now is swelling and the beginning of bruising. Both joints are back where they belong but the tissue around them has been through something and it knows it. He'll be stiff tomorrow in a way that will make him think something is still wrong." She straightened. "Nothing will be still wrong. That's just the tissue complaining. It's allowed."

She pulled a length of cloth from the supply she'd laid out and began folding it into a sling with the efficiency of someone who had done this particular fold so many times her hands did it without instruction.

"You asked because you wanted to be useful," she said. It wasn't an accusation. "Knowing what you're looking at makes you more useful. That's a reasonable instinct." She moved to fit the sling. "Most people who come in here to help me don't ask. They look at the wall or they look at the patient and they try very hard not to see either one."

She glanced up briefly.

"You looked."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lift my hands from his shoulders slowly, my arms stiff. "I look at a lot of things," I say, my voice rough. "Don't mean I understand them." I help her settle the sling over his good arm. "What do you need me to do now?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge let him help with the sling without commenting on whether he was doing it correctly. He was doing it correctly. She moved to the other arm and began the second one.

"There's a crate under the left side of the table," she said. "Blanket on top. When we're done here you're going to get him into it and keep him from standing up for the next twenty minutes." She pulled the fold through and checked the angle. "He's going to want to stand up. He's going to feel better than he should and he's going to want to prove it. You're going to be unimpressed."

She tied off the second sling and stepped back and looked at both of them together. Even. The right angle. She adjusted the left by two degrees and then left it alone.

"After that I need the table." She said it without apology. There wasn't a version of this work that had room for apology in it. "There's a man outside who's been waiting longer than he should have because this took longer than I'd planned."

She began stripping the cloth from her hands, the pieces she'd wrapped to keep her grip clean, dropping them into the bucket at the foot of the table.

"You said you'd rather know than imagine it." She said it to the bucket, then looked up. "That's going to be useful to you if you're staying. Imagination in a place like this is expensive and it spends you in the wrong direction." She picked up the lamp and trimmed the wick, which had been bothering her since she'd walked in. "Knowing is cheaper. Knowing you can work with."

She set the lamp back down. The light improved slightly. Not much.

"Can you stay."

It wasn't quite a question. It had the shape of one but she was already looking toward the tent flap when she said it, already thinking about the man outside.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped looking at the tent flap.

She looked at Wick instead, and the look lasted long enough to mean something. Not suspicion. More like recalibration.

"Shrapnel is metal moving fast through tissue that isn't built for metal," she said. "It doesn't cut the way a blade cuts. A blade moves through along one line and the damage is along that line. Shrapnel tumbles." She turned back to the table and began stripping the cloth from it, rolling it toward herself in sections. "When it tumbles it tears. The entry wound is small and the path inside is not and the exit wound, if there is one, can be large enough to put your fist in. Not always. Depends on the piece, depends on the angle, depends on what it hit along the way."

She dropped the cloth over the side.

"What it hits along the way is the problem." She said it evenly, the way she'd say anything. "Bowel is the worst in terms of what it does to the timeline. Bowel perforates and you don't always know it immediately and the man feels bad and then feels better and then feels much worse and by the time he feels much worse you're behind. Vessels are the worst in terms of speed. Artery goes and you have minutes and the minutes are not negotiable." She moved to the head of the table and began resetting it, straightening the surface. "Lung sits somewhere in the middle. Lung I can sometimes do something about. Lung has bought me time before."

She paused with her hands flat on the table.

"Shrapnel also stays," she said. "The body walls it off. A man can carry pieces of metal in him for thirty years and die of something else entirely. I leave pieces in when getting them out would cost more than leaving them." She said it without defensiveness. It was just the accounting. "I have left pieces in men who thanked me for it later and pieces in men who didn't survive to have an opinion. The calculation is the same either time."

She looked at Wick.

"You're asking because the man outside has shrapnel," she said. "Or because you've seen shrapnel and you're trying to build a map after the fact." She didn't ask which. "Either way the answer is the same, so it doesn't matter."

She pulled the lamp closer to the center of the table.

"Go get him."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content:
I nod, moving past the table to the tent flap. Outside, the night air is sharp. The man leaning against the supply cart looks pale. His hands are clamped over his side, and the fabric is dark and wet.

I keep my voice low. "She's ready for you." I duck under his arm, shoulder taking his weight. "Just walk."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard them before she saw them. The particular rhythm of two people moving as one unit, one set of footsteps working and one set being managed. She'd learned to hear the difference years ago. She turned the lamp up as far as it would go and pulled the second stool to the side of the table where she'd want it.

The man came through the tent flap and she looked at him the way she looked at everything. Pale, yes. Hands on his side, which meant he knew where it hurt and was trying to hold it together in the literal sense, the body's instinct to apply pressure to the thing that felt like it was coming apart. The fabric was dark from mid-waist to hip. She tracked the spread of it and did the arithmetic.

"Table," she said. Not to the man. To Wick.

She moved to meet them, got her hand under the man's free arm, and helped transfer his weight from Wick to the table's edge. She didn't ask him how he was feeling. She never asked that. She could see how he was feeling.

"What's your name," she said, getting him turned, getting him down onto the surface.

She wasn't waiting for the answer before she started. Her hands were already at his side, moving his hands away from the wound, replacing them with her own. The pressure he'd been applying was good instinct and bad information. She needed to see it.

"Tell me what happened," she said. "Not for sympathy. I need to know the direction."

She got the fabric away from the wound and looked at what was there. She looked at it for a long moment without speaking, her face doing nothing in particular.

"Hold the lamp closer," she said to Wick. "Left side, angle it down."

Her thumbs were already moving along the edge of the wound, reading it, the way she'd read the shoulders. The entry was ragged, which told her something. The size told her something else. She pressed two fingers in a slow circle around it, watching the man's face in her peripheral vision, mapping his pain against the geography of what might be underneath.

"You did right, keeping pressure on it," she said to the man. She said it because it was true and because truth was the only comfort she dealt in. "That bought you time. You're using the time now."

She looked up at Wick over the lamp.

"Tell me what you saw when it happened. Where he was standing, what direction the blast came from." She kept her fingers where they were. "The wound tells me where it is. You tell me where it came from. Between the two of us we find out where it went."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up.

"Irrigating," she said. "Flushing the wound with clean water before I do anything else because if I go in without flushing I'm pushing whatever was on that shrapnel further in. That's what's burning him." She kept the stream steady, controlled, the same pressure throughout. "It's going to burn for another thirty seconds and then I'm going to stop and it's going to feel better and he's going to think the worst is over."

She stopped. Set the irrigation aside.

"It's not over," she said. "I'm telling him and I'm telling you."

She picked up the probe. It was a thin thing, blunt-tipped, and she had used it so many times she no longer thought about it as a separate object. It was just an extension of what her fingers were already doing.

"Probing now," she said. "I'm trying to find the piece without finding it with my fingers, because my fingers are too wide and too soft and I'd do more damage than the shrapnel did. This is slower than it looks like it should be." She felt the man try to come off the table and didn't stop. "Hold his hips. Not his shoulders, his hips. He's going to try to curl and if he curls I lose my angle."

She found resistance. Stopped. Redirected two degrees.

"There's one piece that I can feel and I don't know yet if there's more. The one I can feel is sitting against something hard, which is either rib or good luck, and I'm going to know which in about twenty seconds." She kept the probe moving, small increments, reading what came back through the handle the way she read everything. "If it's rib the piece hasn't gone deep enough to find anything important and I can get it out and pack the wound and he's going to be miserable for six weeks and then he's going to be fine. If it's not rib I'm going to tell you that too and we're going to have a different conversation."

The probe found the edge of the piece. She mapped it. Once, twice, a third time.

"It's rib," she said.

She said it the same way she said everything. But she said it.

"Getting the piece out now. This is the part where he's going to feel like I'm killing him and I'm not killing him. I need him to stay flat and I need your weight on his hips and I need you to keep talking to me so I know you're still with me." She picked up the forceps and got her angle. "What did you see. Direction of the blast. Tell me now, give me something to work with while I do this."

Her hands didn't waver. They never wavered. She had learned a long time ago that the hands had to be a separate country from everything else, and she had made them that, and she did not think about what that had cost her because there was no percentage in it.

"Talking," she said. "Now. Keep going."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: My arms shake against his thrashing. "From the east ridge." My voice feels tight. "He was facing north when it hit. Heard it before he saw it." I lock my elbows. *Rib, she said. Rib is good.* "Shrapnel came from his left side. Low."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge filed it.

"Left side, low, facing north, blast from east ridge." She was already adjusting her angle as she said it, the new information folding into what her hands were already telling her. "That tracks. Entry's consistent with low-left origin." The forceps were in and she was moving them the way she moved everything, slow and deliberate and without apology. "Means it traveled lateral to medial. Means I'm looking at one piece with a clean path and not a scatter pattern."

The man was making sounds she'd stopped cataloguing four years ago.

"Hold," she said.

She had the piece. She could feel it, the particular feedback of metal in the grip of metal, different from tissue, different from bone. She kept the angle and she kept the pressure and she did not hurry.

"Still one piece," she said. "That's the blast direction telling me something useful. Close-scatter gives you fragments. Distance gives you one piece moving fast." She turned the forceps a quarter rotation, working with the wound's angle rather than against it. "You gave me good information. That mattered."

She extracted the piece in one continuous motion and dropped it into the basin without looking at it. She'd look at it later. Right now she looked at the wound.

"Packing next," she said. "This is going to feel like less than what came before and it's still going to be bad." She was already reaching for the gauze. "Talk to him. Not comfort. Just words. Something that keeps his attention in this tent."

She began packing, methodical, layer by layer.

"He's going to live," she said. She said it the way she said everything. Flat and without decoration, because decoration would have made it smaller somehow, would have made it a thing she was performing rather than a thing she was reporting. "Six weeks like I said. He's going to be angry about it around week three and that's fine. Anger at week three means he's healing."

She pressed the last layer in and held it.

"Tell me your hands are still on him."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't tell him to get up.

She finished tying off the dressing, checked the tension, checked it again. Then she set her instruments in the basin in the order she'd need to clean them and she looked at Wick on the floor of her tent and she pulled the second stool over and sat down on it, which put her roughly at his level, which was not an accident.

The man on the table was breathing. She could hear it. She didn't need to look.

"Say the rest," she repeated. Not mocking. Just making sure she had the question right. "You mean what I didn't say while I was working."

She put her hands on her knees. They were still the hands she'd made into a separate country, and she was aware of them, and she left them where they were.

"I don't know what the rest is until you tell me what you're carrying," she said. "I'm not a priest. I don't do general absolution." She looked at him directly. The lamp was better now that she'd trimmed it and his face was clear. "You've seen shrapnel before tonight. You said so without saying so. You wanted a map after the fact." She didn't make it a question. "That's someone specific. That's not a general education."

She waited.

The tent made its sounds around them. Canvas and wind and the man on the table breathing in and out with the reliability of a man who was going to keep doing it for a long time.

"I've been doing this four years," she said, when the silence had gone on long enough that she thought he might need something to push against. "I have held men down the way you held him down and I have held men down who didn't come off the table the way he came off the table, and I have had people sitting where you're sitting who needed to say something and didn't know how to start." She wasn't gentle about it. Gentle wasn't the right tool. "The way you start is you just say the first true thing. Not the whole thing. Just the first piece of it, and then the next piece, and it goes the same way the probe goes. Small increments. You find out what's there by going slowly."

She looked at her hands.

"I told you I'd tell you when I was managing someone toward a comfortable end and why." She looked back up. "Same principle. I don't let people sit on the floor of my tent in the middle of the night and say *say the rest* and then talk around what they mean. That's not a kindness. That's just a longer way of being alone."

She waited again. She was good at waiting. Four years had made her good at it.

"So," she said. "First true thing."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "He was lying on his back in the dirt," I start, my voice low. "They brought him in with the other walking wounded. There was a hole in his side, about like that." I nod toward the table. "Wasn't bleeding much. He could talk." I look at my own hands. "They said he was fine. He said he was fine. I believed it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't move.

She listened the way she listened to the probe, to the feedback through the handle, to the thing the information was telling her underneath the information.

"When did he stop being fine," she said.

Not *did he.* She already knew he had. That was the only shape this story had.

She didn't look away from Wick's face. She'd found that people needed to be looked at when they said things like this, not because it helped them feel better but because looking away was a kind of verdict, and she wasn't in the business of verdicts.

"Wasn't bleeding much," she said, and she said it back to him the same way he'd said it, not to be cruel, just so he could hear it outside his own head. "That's the one that gets people. The ones that bleed a lot look like what they are. The ones that don't bleed much look like something else." She kept her hands on her knees. "Bowel. I said bowel earlier. That's the one that doesn't bleed much at the start."

She let that sit.

"He could talk," she said. "He said he was fine. You believed him because he was giving you the information a fine man gives you, and you had no reason to weight your own doubt against his testimony and his ability to stand upright and form sentences." She said it plainly. "That's not a failure of attention. That's a wound that knows how to lie."

The lamp moved slightly in a draft from somewhere and the shadows shifted and settled.

"How long," she said. "Between when they brought him in and when you knew."

She asked it because she needed to know, and because he needed to say it, and because those two things were the same thing right now. The probe going slowly. Small increments. You found out what was there by not stopping.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Two hours." I swallow. My throat is dry. "He stopped talking first. Then he started shivering. Then he just...looked at the ceiling and didn't look away."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was quiet for a moment.

Not the quiet of someone searching for something to say. The quiet of someone who had received a piece of information and was being accurate about what it meant.

"Two hours is inside the window," she said. "I want you to hear that. Two hours from presentation to recognition is inside the window where things can still go one way or the other. It's not comfortable time. It's not time you'd choose. But it's not the time where the outcome was already written and you were just watching it happen." She paused. "I'm telling you that because it's true, not because it helps."

She looked at her hands and then back at him.

"The shivering is the body losing the argument," she said. "Temperature regulation goes when the blood isn't moving the way it should be moving. That's not something you can see coming from the outside. That's interior. That's the body keeping its own books and not showing you the ledger until it's already in deficit." She said it evenly. "The ceiling thing is the grey country. I told you about that earlier. He wasn't gone when he was looking at the ceiling. He was somewhere else, which is a thing the body does to make the last part bearable."

She stopped.

She looked at Wick on the floor of her tent, his hands in his lap, the way he'd looked at them, and she thought about what the next thing was and whether she was going to say it.

She said it.

"You're going to want there to be something you should have done," she said. "You're going to go looking for it. The moment you should have pushed back when he said he was fine, the moment you should have known the shivering meant something different than cold, the moment you should have found someone like me two hours earlier." She didn't soften it. "You're going to look for that thing because having a thing you did wrong is easier than having a thing that was just true. A mistake means it could have gone differently. A mistake means you had the power and used it badly." She held his gaze. "But sometimes there's no mistake. Sometimes it's just a wound that lies and a man who believed what he was told and two hours that moved the way two hours move."

The man on the table breathed in and out.

"I don't know which one it was for you," she said. "I wasn't there. But I know that you're sitting on the floor of my tent instead of outside it, which means you're not done yet, which means you're going to have to find a way to carry it." She put her hands back on her knees. "So I'm asking you. When you looked for the mistake. Did you find one. A real one. Not a feeling. An actual thing you knew and didn't act on."

She waited.

"Because that answer matters," she said. "And I'll tell you why it matters after you give it to me."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at my hands like they're someone else's. "I'm a soldier. I follow orders. The orders were *he's fine, move on*." My throat clicks. "So I moved on."
