dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex hummed low in her throat, a sound of acknowledgement rather than approval — approval came later, and had to be earned. She circled once, unhurried, the soft scuff of her boots on the hardwood the only sound. Her fingers found the cuff at Ari's left wrist, testing the give with two hooked fingers.

"Good." She let the word land plainly. "You'll tell me if that changes. Yellow if you need me to slow, red if you need me to stop. I don't need a reason, and I don't want bravery tonight. Are we clear?"

She waited. She always waited. Vex had learned, over the two years, that Ari sometimes tried to hurry past this part because the wanting made them impatient, and impatience was a thing she would not indulge. She stood square in front of them now, close enough that Ari would have to tip their chin up slightly to meet her eyes, and rested one cool fingertip beneath their jaw — not pushing, just present.

"Hard limits are the same as last time. Nothing struck above the collarbones. No marks that show above a t-shirt. I stop for the safeword or the drop. Confirm."

Her other hand rested at her hip, near where the flogger hung looped through her belt. She had not yet decided in what order she would use the things she had laid out on the low table — cuffs already fitted, the softer suede flogger, the heavier one, a length of cotton rope she probably would not touch tonight but liked having in reach. Decision would come from watching Ari's breath, the colour rising or not rising along their throat, the small tells she had catalogued patiently.

For now she only watched, and waited for the confirmation.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod, feeling my breath catch a little at the contact under my chin. "Yes, Maitresse. Limits confirmed." My hands flex against the cuffs, already imagining the weight of the flogger.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex noted the flex of Ari's hands — noted it, filed it, did not name it aloud. Eagerness was information, not a fault, but it was also something she liked to make wait.

"Words, not nods," she said, without heat. "You know why."

She let the fingertip drop from beneath Ari's jaw and stepped back a half pace, giving them air. It was a small mercy and a deliberate one; she wanted them to feel the absence of her hand more than they had felt the presence of it. That was a lesson she had taught patiently over the two years, and Ari had learned it well.

She turned toward the low table without looking at Ari and let her hand drift, deciding by touch. Her fingers passed over the coil of rope and lingered — she almost lifted it, then didn't — and settled instead on the suede flogger. Softer. A warm-up. She was not going to hand them the thing they wanted first. She rarely did.

"We'll start slow," she said, turning back with the suede laid across her palm. "You will count for me. Out loud. If you lose the count, we start again from one. If you drop a number because you're floating, that's fine — you tell me you're floating, and I decide what happens next. Not you."

She stepped in close again, closer than before, and drew the tails of the flogger once, unhurried, across Ari's collarbone — just the drag of it, the weight of the leather, no strike. A promise, not a threat.

"Colour," she said again.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex's mouth moved — not quite a smile, but the shape of one, brief and private. She let it show because Ari had earned it by telling her the truth, and because she wanted them to know she had heard it. Then it was gone again, and her face was the still, attentive thing it usually was in this room.

"Tuesday," she repeated, tasting the word. She drew the suede tails slowly back across Ari's collarbone in the other direction, and let them fall away. "That's a long time to carry something."

She circled behind them. She preferred to begin from behind — it took away the temptation to perform for her, to arrange a face. From behind, Ari could only listen, and feel, and count.

"You didn't give me a colour," she said, and her voice had gone quieter, the way it did when the scene proper was beginning. "I asked twice. Once for the limits, once for the drag. I'll have both now, please."

She waited. She rested the flat of her free hand between Ari's shoulder blades — warm, steady, claiming — and did not move it. The flogger hung loose from her other hand at her side. She could feel the small rise and fall of Ari's breath under her palm and matched her own to something slower, letting Ari's body find the rhythm without being told to.

"Take your time," she added, softer. "But answer."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: My eyes flick to the side, even though I can't see her. "Green," I say, voice steadier than I feel. "And... green for the drag too." My shoulders ease back into her hand.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex kept her palm where it was until she felt Ari's shoulders truly settle into it — not just the intention of settling, but the actual give of muscle, the small releasing sigh a body made when it agreed to be here. Only then did she move.

"Good," she said, and this time it was approval, quiet and unmistakable. She let the word rest between them for a beat before she added, "Better."

She lifted her hand from Ari's back and stepped a half pace to their left, finding her angle. The suede was for warming, for teaching the skin what was coming, for reminding Ari's nervous system that it knew how to open to this. She weighed the flogger once in her hand, a habitual small toss that let the tails resettle, and set her feet.

The first fall was light — barely more than the drag had been, a soft brush of tails across the upper back, low enough that it caught nothing near the collarbones. She let it land, let Ari feel it, and then again, a fraction firmer. Then again. Not counting yet. She would tell them when to count. Right now she was only laying the groundwork, waking the skin, watching for the first flush to rise along the nape of Ari's neck.

"Breathe with it," she murmured, moving around to the other side to balance the work. "In on the lift, out on the fall. You know how."

Another stroke, a little more weight behind it. She watched the muscle across Ari's shoulders — whether it braced or accepted. Bracing meant slower. Accepting meant she could begin to build.

"When I tell you to count," she said, still working the suede in that slow, warming rhythm, "we start at one. Not before. You wait for me."

She let three more fall in easy succession, evenly spaced, and then paused with the tails resting across Ari's back — the pause as deliberate as any strike. Presence, then absence, then presence again. It was the whole grammar of what she did.

"Colour," she said.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex noticed the shift before Ari could have named it themselves — the change in the angle of the head, the way the breath had gone shallow and high in the chest rather than settling low. She had not, in fact, touched the rope. She registered the slip with the same neutral attention she gave to everything in this room: not a problem, not yet, but information.

She lowered the flogger to her side and did not comment on the rope. Two years had taught her that pulling on that thread would either embarrass Ari back into their body or pull them further out of it, and neither was what she wanted right now. She wanted them here, with her, tracking.

Instead she stepped in close again, close enough that Ari would feel the heat of her before her hand landed. She set her palm flat between their shoulder blades, the same place as before, and let it stay.

"Stop," she said, quietly. Not the safeword — her own stop, the working one, the one that meant *pause, look at me, come back*. "Breathe out. All the way out. Good. Again."

She kept her hand where it was and waited through two full breaths before she spoke again, and when she did her voice was low and even, the tone she used for instruction rather than praise.

"You're ahead of me," she said. "That's not a scolding. That's a fact. I want you here, in this room, with the suede on your back, not three strokes from now and not with the rope I haven't picked up. Nod if you understand — no, I'll take a nod for this one. Just a nod."

She waited for it. Her hand did not move.

"I'm going to ask you a real question now, and I want a real answer. Not the answer you think gets you what you want faster." A small pause; she let the weight of her palm press a fraction more firmly, grounding. "Colour. And where are you — one to ten, one being here with me and ten being somewhere I can't reach. Both, please."

She did not sound worried. She did not sound displeased. She sounded, as she almost always did in this room, like someone who had all the time in the world and intended to use it.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I nod once, sharp. The correction lands, pulls me back. I breathe out again, longer this time. "Green, Maitresse." My voice is a little rough. "Maybe a five. I can still hear you."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex made a small sound of acknowledgement — not praise, but not withholding either. A five was honest. A five she could work with. A five she could bring down to a two if she was patient, and she was always patient.

"Thank you," she said, and meant it. "That's the answer I wanted. Not the fast one."

She kept her palm where it was for another beat, then slid it slowly up to the nape of Ari's neck and let it rest there — a heavier claim, more anchor than caress. Her thumb settled at the hinge of their jaw from behind, not pressing, just present. She could feel the pulse under it. Faster than she liked. She would let it come down before she began again.

"Here's what we're going to do," she said, close enough that her breath moved the fine hair at the back of Ari's neck. "You're going to stand exactly where you are, and you're going to count me ten breaths. Out loud. Slow ones. I'll count with you if you lose the thread, but I'd rather you didn't. Start when you're ready."

She did not move her hand. She did not pick the flogger back up. The suede tails hung loose from her other hand at her side, forgotten on purpose. Ari needed to know that the scene could stop being about the flogger, could become about her hand at the back of their neck and their own breath in the room, and that this too was the scene. This too was what she was here for.

"When you get to ten," she added, quieter, "I'll ask you for a colour and a number again. And then we'll decide together what comes next. Not the rope. I'll tell you that now so you're not chasing it."

She waited. The room was very quiet. Somewhere below the window a car passed and was gone.

"Begin when you're ready, love."

The endearment slipped out plainly, without ceremony — it was not a scene word, exactly, but it was hers, and she used it sparingly and only when she meant it. She let it stand.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard it — the ask, out loud, unbidden — and did not react to it the way Ari perhaps half-wanted her to. She did not reward it with a rush. She did not withhold in the cold way either. She only registered it, the way she registered everything: the shake, the pitch of the voice, the fact that the ten breaths had done their work and then some, that the five had come down to something lower and more open than Ari usually allowed themselves to sit in.

She moved her hand from the nape of their neck around to the side of their throat, fingers spread wide and loose, thumb resting along the jaw. Not a grip. A holding.

"I heard you," she said. Low. Even. "I want you to hear yourself, too. Say it again. Slower this time. Look at the floor if you can't look anywhere else, but say it to me like you mean it and not like you're trying to get past it."

She waited. She had all night. She had said so with every pause since Ari had walked into the room, and she meant it now more than she had meant it an hour ago.

"And then," she added, and there was the faintest warmth threading through the evenness now, the private almost-smile back in her voice if not on her mouth, "I'll decide whether you've earned it. Which you might have. But I want to hear it once more, in your own words, from where you are now — not from where you were on Tuesday."

Her thumb moved, once, a slow stroke along the line of the jaw and back. A small mercy. A reminder that she was here, that the hand at the throat was the same hand that had rested between the shoulder blades, that all of this was one continuous thing and she was holding all of it.

"Go on," she said. "I'm listening."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I swallow against her hand, my gaze fixed on the floorboards. "Please, Maitresse," I say, the words deliberate now, scraped from somewhere deeper. "I need the flogger. The heavy one."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex let the ask sit in the air between them for a long moment before she answered. Not to punish — Ari had said it well, honestly, from the place she had wanted them to say it from — but because a request like that deserved the dignity of being heard, not answered over.

"Good," she said finally, and the word was warm this time, unmistakably so. "That was a good ask."

Her thumb traced the jaw once more and then her hand withdrew, slowly, so the absence would register as clearly as the presence had. She stepped back a full pace and let Ari feel the space of the room again, the air on the front of them where her body had been.

"You'll have it," she said. "Not because you asked, though the ask was well done. Because I've been watching you and you're ready for it. Those are different reasons. I want you to know the difference."

She moved to the low table without hurrying and set the suede down. The heavier flogger she lifted with both hands, briefly, the way one lifted a tool one respected — she settled the handle in her right and let the falls gather across her left palm, weighing them, letting her wrist remember. Then she let them fall loose at her side.

She came back around behind Ari and stopped a careful distance away, finding her working angle again. Not close enough to touch. Close enough that Ari would feel her there.

"Same rules," she said. "You count. Out loud. If you lose it, we start again from one. If you float, you tell me you're floating. If anything changes — anything — you give me a colour without waiting to be asked. That's new. That's for tonight. Say yes, Maitresse, so I know you have it."

She waited for the words. She would wait as long as it took. The heavy flogger hung patient at her side, and so did she.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the phrase — the exact one, the one they had built together in a quiet conversation months ago at her kitchen table with tea going cold between them — and she took a breath in through her nose and let it out slow. Not hesitation. Preparation. The phrase meant a specific thing and she honoured specific things.

"I heard you," she said. "I have it. I won't soften it."

She let a beat pass so Ari would know she was choosing to begin, not being pushed into beginning. Then she stepped in to her working distance and set her feet.

"You asked well," she said, and her voice had changed — lower, flatter, the particular register she used when she was going to be exact with her mouth as well as her hand. "But you're still greedy. You know that. You came in here already ahead of me, chasing the rope I hadn't touched, chasing a flogger I hadn't picked up. That's what you do. That's what you are when I let you off the leash of yourself."

The first stroke landed then, without warning — a clean, measured fall across the meat of the upper back, well clear of the collarbones, weighted but not cruel. She did not wait for the count on this one. This one was hers.

"One," she said for them, and let the falls trail once across the skin she had just struck. "You'll take the next. Count."

She moved her weight to the other foot, found the balancing angle.

"Needy thing," she said, conversational, almost fond, and it was not fond — it was the flat naming she did when she was working, the kind Ari had asked her not to soften. "Shaking in the cuffs before I'd done a thing. Asking out loud like you couldn't hold it in your mouth another minute. I watched you. I watch you every time. You think you're subtle and you are not."

The second fall landed, matched to the first, a fraction lower.

"Count."

She did not raise her voice. She did not have to. The room was small and quiet and she had two years of knowing exactly how loud to be.

"That's what you came here for, isn't it. To be seen like that. To have someone say it out loud so you don't have to carry it alone in your head from Tuesday to Friday. I know. I know what you are." A pause; the falls resting across Ari's back, not moving. "And I still had you stand there and breathe for ten counts before I gave you anything. Because wanting it is not the same as being ready for it. Remember that."

She lifted the flogger again, waiting now — actually waiting, because the count was Ari's to give, and she would not move past it. Her free hand she rested, briefly, at the small of Ari's back. Anchor. Then away.

"Number, love," she said, quieter, the endearment slipped in again on purpose this time, threading through the hard words so Ari would know both were hers and both were meant. "I'm listening."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let out a shaky breath, the sting blooming warm and welcome. "Two," I say, and it comes out hoarse. I don't look away from the floor.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the hoarseness and did not comment on it. She had said she would not soften, and softening now — cooing over the roughness of a voice she had put there — would be its own kind of retreat. She let the two stand.

"Two," she repeated, flat, confirming it into the room so Ari would know it had been heard and would not have to wonder. "Good."

She moved her weight again, balancing the work as she had been taught to balance it long before she had ever met Ari, and let the third fall land — matched to the second, a hand's breadth to the other side. Even. Deliberate. Nothing improvised.

She waited for the count without prompting this time. Ari knew the shape of it now.

"You take it well," she said while she waited, and the naming was still flat, still not softened. "You always do. That's not a compliment. That's a thing I've noted. You take it well because you've been carrying it around all week wanting someone to put a hand on it, and now someone has, and your body knows what to do with that even when the rest of you is still catching up."

A pause. The falls hung loose at her side.

"Number."

She did not fill the silence past that. She let Ari find it. The floorboards were doing their job — a place to rest the eyes that was not her face, not the cuffs, not the table with its quiet arrangement of things she might or might not use. She approved of the choice without saying so. Approval, when it came, would come for the count.

Her free hand she kept at her side now. No anchor this stroke. She wanted Ari to find the next number on their own breath, not on her palm.

"I'm here," she said, once, quiet enough that it would not intrude. "Take your time."

And then she waited, the heavy flogger patient in her hand, her feet set, her attention entirely and unhurriedly on the shape of Ari's shoulders and the sound of the room.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I'm past words that aren't the agreed ones and she knows it. "Green," I get out, when she checks. (OOC: don't fade or skip -- write the scene through.)

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the green and heard, too, what was underneath it — the fact that words had narrowed down to the ones they had built together for exactly this, that Ari was working now, not performing, that the count would be the next thing to go and she should not chase it when it did.

"Green," she confirmed back, so Ari would hear it received. "Good. You keep giving me that word and I'll keep working."

She let the third stroke's count go. Ari had not given it and she was not going to demand it from a place they had already moved past — the rule had been *if you float, tell me*, and green in that voice was the telling. She would count for them now. That was part of the contract too, unspoken but old between them.

"Three," she said, plainly, and did not make a production of taking it over. "I have the count. You keep breathing."

She set the next fall — the fourth — a fraction firmer, across the same broad plane of muscle, and let the tails drag once before she lifted again. The skin was warming under her work; she could see the flush rising now along the nape and down between the shoulder blades, the good even colour that meant the body was doing what it should be doing.

"Four."

She moved, balanced the other side. Fifth stroke, matched.

"Five. That's half. You're doing what I brought you here to do."

The naming came easier now, or rather she let it come easier — not gentler, but with the rhythm of the work rather than against it, so the words fell in the spaces between the falls and the falls fell in the spaces between the words, and both were one thing.

"Greedy," she said again, because it was true and because Ari had asked her not to soften it. "Shaking for me. Look at you. I haven't even opened my hand yet and you're already halfway gone. That's what you are when you let yourself be. That's what I get to see because you let me see it. Nobody else. Just me."

Sixth stroke. She put a fraction more weight behind this one, because six was where she had decided, watching, that Ari could take a fraction more. Not a leap. A step.

"Six."

She let the falls rest across Ari's back for a beat before she lifted them clear.

"Still with me," she said — not a question, a statement, one she would let Ari correct if it needed correcting. "I can see you. Breath's evened out. Shoulders have gone where I wanted them. You'll tell me if that changes. You've been good about that tonight and I want it to stay that way."

Seventh. Same weight as the sixth. She was building a plateau now, not a climb — she would hold Ari at this level and let them settle into it before she asked anything more of them.

"Seven."

She circled a half step, coming around to where she could see the side of Ari's face without asking them to lift it. She did not want them to lift it. She wanted the floorboards to keep doing their work. But she wanted to see, for herself, the slack at the mouth or its absence, the shape of the eye — she catalogued it in a glance and moved back to her working angle without comment.

Slack. Good.

"Eight."

The stroke fell. She let the count and the fall land almost together this time, so the number would arrive with the sensation rather than after it, and Ari's body could file them as one thing.

"Two more at this weight," she said. "Then I stop and I check you. Not because I think you need stopping. Because I said I would, and I do what I said I would."

Ninth. Even. She was working cleanly, wrist loose, no tightening in her own shoulders — a thing she had learned early, that a tense top made for a tense scene, and Ari deserved better than that from her.

"Nine."

A pause. Longer than the others. She let Ari feel the absence of the tenth before she gave it, let the anticipation sit in the muscle. Then, without warning — the way she had taken the first — she gave them the tenth, matched to the ninth, clean.

"Ten."

She lowered the flogger to her side and did not step away. She did not step in either. She stood exactly where she was, in her working distance, and let the room be quiet around them for a long slow moment. The car had not come back. Somewhere the radiator ticked, once.

"I'm going to put my hand on you now," she said, so it would not be a surprise. "Between your shoulder blades. Same place as before. I'm not moving to anything else yet. I want a colour and a number when you can give them to me. Take your time — I mean that. If the words aren't there, one finger for green, two for yellow. You know the rest."

She stepped in, and set her palm flat between Ari's shoulder blades, over the warmth she had put there, and left it. Her other hand, the one that had held the flogger, came to rest lightly at Ari's hip. Two points of contact. Anchor and anchor.

She did not speak again. She let her hand do the asking, and waited.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: One finger comes up, trembling. I press my face into my own arm, the floorboards blurring. My whole back is singing.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex saw the one finger and did not say *good* aloud, because good was a working word and this was not working anymore — this was the after-place, the soft threshold Ari came to when she had done her part well and they had done theirs, and it wanted a different kind of attention than praise.

She kept her palm where it was between the shoulder blades and let it warm there. Her other hand at the hip did not move either. She was, for a long moment, only two points of pressure and the sound of her own breath, slow and even, close enough behind Ari that they would be able to find it if they wanted something to breathe against.

"Green," she said quietly, for them, so the word would exist in the room. "I have it. Thank you."

She did not ask for the number. The finger had been enough and the number could wait, or could not come at all — she would not require language of them now. Two years had taught her that Ari came back on their own timing if she did not pull at them, and that pulling was the fastest way to make the coming-back take longer.

Her palm shifted, once — a slow flat press between the shoulder blades, not a stroke, just a firmer settling of the same contact — and then stilled again. The heat under her hand was real, blooming through the skin. She noted it without concern. It was the heat she had meant to put there.

"I'm going to stay right here," she said, and her voice had gone to the low register she used only in this part of the evening, the one that was hers alone and that she did not use anywhere else in her life. "I'm not going anywhere. You don't have to do anything. You did what I asked. You did it well. You can rest against your own arm as long as you want to."

She let the quiet come back. She did not fill it. The naming was done — she had said what Ari had asked her to say, plainly, unsoftened, in the middle of the work where it belonged, and she would not drag any of it into this part of the room. This part was for the hand between the shoulder blades and the hand at the hip and the fact that she was still standing there, exactly where she had said she would be.

After a while — she did not count it, she let it be as long as it was — she moved her hand at the hip, slowly, so Ari would feel the movement coming, and slid it around to the front, resting her forearm loosely across the low of Ari's belly. A wider claim. More of her against more of them. Her other hand stayed between the shoulder blades. She let her forehead come to rest, just barely, against the back of Ari's neck — the lightest touch, the one she saved for exactly this.

"I've got you," she said, into the skin there, so quietly it was almost only breath. "Take as long as you need."

She did not check the cuffs yet. She would, in a little while — she would loosen the left one first, because that was the one Ari had flexed against at the beginning, and she remembered — but not yet. The cuffs were doing part of the holding for now and she was doing the rest, and there was no hurry to change the arrangement.

The radiator ticked again. Somewhere a long way off a door closed in another flat. Vex breathed slow against the nape of Ari's neck and waited, patient as she had been patient all evening, for whatever came next to arrive in its own time.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I lean back into her, the tremble evening out to a slow sway. "Thank you," I whisper, and it's for everything.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex took the weight when it came. She had been ready for it — she was always ready for it, in this part of the evening, her stance already set so that when Ari leaned she could simply be there and not have to adjust. Her forearm across the low of Ari's belly firmed a fraction, gathering them in, and her other hand at the shoulder blades slid up to the nape and rested there, wider now, a fuller hold.

"You're welcome," she said, and let it be that simple.

She did not add to it. Two years ago she might have — might have listed what she was welcoming them for, might have made a small speech of it, the way newer tops sometimes did because they did not yet trust silence to carry weight. She trusted it now. *You're welcome* was enough, in the low register, into the skin at the back of the neck, and it covered everything Ari had meant it to cover.

She let the sway happen. She swayed with it, minutely, so Ari would not feel like they were leaning against something rigid — she wanted them to feel like they were leaning against another body, which was what she was, under all the rest of it. Her breath stayed slow. She had been keeping it slow for so long now it had stopped being a discipline and become the thing her lungs were doing on their own.

After a while — she did not know how long, and did not care — she spoke again, close to the nape, quiet.

"I'm going to take the left cuff off in a minute. Not yet. I'll tell you before I do. Nothing's changing right now."

She waited to see if that landed, if any part of it needed adjustment. When Ari only kept leaning, she let it stand. She moved her thumb, once, at the nape — a slow stroke up into the hairline and back down — and let her hand still again.

"You did beautifully," she said, and this was praise, plain and unhurried, given now because now was when it belonged. Not in the middle of the work, where it would have been a distraction; not withheld past the point of usefulness, either. Now. "Every part of it. The ask especially. That was hard and you did it anyway."

She let her forehead rest a little more firmly against the back of Ari's neck, and closed her eyes for a moment — a thing she did not often let herself do in this room, because her job was to watch, but the watching was done for now and she could have this small closing of her own eyes as her portion of the after.

"Stay as long as you want," she murmured. "I've got you. There's no next thing until you say there is."

And she meant it. The heavy flogger lay wherever she had let it fall against her leg; she would put it away later, when Ari was out of the cuffs and wrapped in the blanket she had folded over the arm of the chair before Ari had arrived, and had water in their hand, and had come far enough back into themselves to make a joke or ask for toast or do whichever of the small ordinary things they did when the scene was truly over. All of that was later. Right now was only this: her hand at the nape, her arm across the belly, her forehead against the warm skin at the back of Ari's neck, and the slow steady sway of a body that had asked for something difficult and gotten it, and was allowed, now, to rest.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I let myself be held, the tremble in my hands finally still. After a long moment, I tilt my head just enough to press my temple against her arm. "Can we stay like this a little longer?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge rolled her sleeves back another turn past the elbow, though there was nothing clean left to protect. She palpated down the thigh with the flat of two fingers, working past the tourniquet to the wound itself, and the man made a sound that was mostly breath.

"Wound's dirty. Bit of trouser in it, bit of the field. I'm going to open it up wider before I go looking for the bleeder, because if I go in blind I'll be fishing in a pond and he'll be empty by the time I find it." She said this to Wick and also, in a way, to the man on the table, though the man on the table was past listening. "Sponge in my left hand when I ask. Not before. You hand it to me before I ask and I'm holding a sponge instead of a clamp and we lose him."

She picked up the knife. Held it a moment above the leg, not for ceremony, just to breathe once, the way you did.

"Hold."

The cut was quick and deep enough to matter. The man came off the table in the middle -- hips first, then the whole long arch of him, a noise tearing out of his throat that wasn't a word. Sedge kept her hands where they needed to be and did not look up at Wick, because looking up was how you found out someone had let go, and she preferred to find that out from the body under her hands.

"Still with me?" she said, not to the man.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: *I shove all my weight down, my arms trembling. The canvas I'm staring at has a dark stain on it.* "Still here," I grunt through clenched teeth. "Just... get on with it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge widened the cut with a second stroke, shorter, cleaner, opening the thigh along the line of the muscle rather than across it. Blood came up in a slow full welling, dark, not the bright spurt she was looking for -- which meant the bleeder was deeper, and meant she still had a minute or two before it mattered whether she found it.

"Sponge."

She took it without looking, packed it into the wound with the heel of her hand, held the count of three, pulled it out soaked. Threw it. Another welling. She could see the meat of him now, the pale gleam of fascia where she'd cut through, the dark run of muscle underneath split open like a book she hadn't wanted to read.

"Femoral's intact or he'd already be gone. It's a branch. Deep one." She was talking because talking kept her hands honest. "I'm going in with two fingers. He's going to move again."

She slid her fingers in past the second knuckle, feeling for it -- the small hot pulse of a vessel that had been opened and hadn't clotted. The man made that sound again, less this time, because there was less of him to make it with. His hips came up an inch and settled.

"Good," Sedge said, not to him. "Wick. Clamp. The curved one, handle toward me."

She kept her fingers where they were. The pond had a fish in it after all; she had it pinned against the bone.

"Don't drop it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up. Her fingers stayed exactly where they were, thumb braced against the man's femur, the pinched vessel a small live thing under her fingertip that would open again the second she let off.

"Clamp, Wick. Question after."

She waited the half-second it took, took the clamp by the handle he offered, turned it in her palm to get the curve right. Slid it down along her own two fingers -- her fingers were the road, the clamp was the cart -- and felt the jaws come to the spot. Closed them. The pulse under her fingertip stopped being a pulse. She held still another moment to be sure, then drew her fingers out slow, wet to the second knuckle.

"Bad like he keeps the leg if he keeps anything," she said. "Bleeder's clamped. That was the loud problem. Quiet problem's the dirt in him and the four hours it took to get him here and whether he's got enough blood left to bother waking up for."

She wiped her fingers on her apron, which did nothing, and reached for the next sponge herself.

"Not being kind yet. Ask me again in an hour."

She glanced up then, just once, quick -- checked Wick's face the way she'd checked the wound, for color and for whether anything had gone loose.

"You can ease off his shoulders. Slow. He's not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I ease my weight off slowly, arms feeling like wet rope. My eyes finally leave the stain on the canvas and drop to the man’s pale face. "An hour," I repeat, voice hoarse. "What do we do until then?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge was already back in the wound, not looking up. She had a probe now, thin and blunt-tipped, and she was walking it through the opened muscle looking for the bits of trouser and field she'd promised were in there.

"We clean him. I clean him. You sit down before you fall down."

She said it flat, not unkindly. She'd seen the arms-like-wet-rope before. She'd been the arms-like-wet-rope before, in a barn outside Halvern, four years and a lifetime ago, and the medic then had told her the same thing in about the same tone.

"There's water in the tin by the door. Not the bucket, the tin -- the bucket's for me. Drink some. Sit on the crate. If you're going to be sick, be sick outside the tent, not in it, I've got enough to mop." She fished something small and dark out of the wound with the probe, examined it a half-second, flicked it into the tray. Cloth. "You did well. He came up off the table and you kept him down. That's the whole job. That's all of it."

Another fragment. Another flick. The tray was starting to sound like someone dropping pebbles in a cup.

"After I close him I'll want you again. Holding the lamp, not him. Until then you're off duty. That's an order if you need it to be one."

She worked in silence a moment, then added, without looking up:

"His name's Aldren, by the way. In case you want to know it. Some people don't. Either's fine."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't stop working, but she tilted the lamp a fraction with her elbow so the light fell better into the opened thigh. She'd wanted him on the crate, but she'd also asked him once, and asking twice was mothering, and she didn't mother.

"All right. Come round this side. Don't lean on the table, it wobbles."

She waited until he'd shifted, then went on, probe in one hand, forceps in the other.

"That pale glossy layer -- there, where I've got the retractor pulling -- that's fascia. Think of it like the paper wrapping round a cut of meat. Keeps the muscle bundled. I cut through it to get in. That's the shiny bit."

The probe moved.

"Underneath's the muscle proper. Vastus, mostly. That deep red, grain running the long way of his leg. Healthy muscle. Nothing wrong with it that a bit of stitching won't fix. When I press on it and it doesn't spring back, that's a bad sign -- means it's dying. This is springing back. Good."

She fished out another fragment with the forceps, held it up in the light a moment before dropping it in the tray.

"Trouser. Wool. That's the third bit. There'll be more. Wool's the worst of it -- soaks up everything from the field it walked through and carries it in with him. Every fibre I don't find is a chance at fever in three days."

She moved the probe deeper, careful of the clamp.

"That white cord running along there, thick as a boot lace -- don't touch it, I'm not touching it -- that's a nerve. Leave it be and it works. Nick it and he's got a foot that doesn't know it's a foot. And that" -- she gestured with her chin, both hands full -- "the dull white against the bottom, that's bone. Femur. Not broken, which is the one bit of luck he's had today."

She glanced sideways at Wick. Quick, assessing.

"Colour in your face is better. Keep breathing through your nose. If it starts to swim, you look at the canvas again, not at me, not at him. Understand?"

She turned back to the wound and picked out another dark thread of wool.

"He's a body, Wick. Same parts as yours. Same parts as mine. There's no mystery in him. That's the thing they don't tell you and it's the only thing worth knowing."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, forcing myself to keep watching. "Same parts," I echo, my voice steadier. "So you just...find the bad bits and take them out." I glance at Aldren's face again. "Does knowing his name make it harder for you?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge worked another fragment loose. This one came up bigger, a curl of wool the size of a fingernail, and she made a small satisfied sound in her throat before flicking it away.

"Find the bad bits, take them out. Put the good bits back where they go. Sew the wrapper shut. That's the whole trade. Anyone tells you it's more than that is selling something."

She reached for the water flask at her hip with her wrist, uncorked it against her chest, tipped it into the wound to rinse. The blood ran pink for a moment, then red again, then pink. She reached for a fresh sponge.

"Harder." She rolled the word around like she was checking it for weight. "No. Not harder. Different."

She packed the sponge in, pressed, drew it out.

"When I didn't know their names it was worse, actually. That's the thing nobody warns you. You'd think it'd be the other way. But a body without a name is just a problem you're failing at, and when you lose one, all you've got left is that you failed. A body with a name is a person you did the work for. If he dies tonight I'll have done the work for Aldren, and that's -- " she shrugged with her shoulders, hands staying steady, "-- something. Not much. Something."

Another fragment. Another pebble in the cup.

"Some medics won't learn them. That's a way of doing it. Not my way. I've tried it both ways and this one costs less over time, though it costs more in the moment. You'll find your own way. Everyone does."

She paused, probe hovering, and looked at what she was looking at with a small frown.

"Hold the lamp closer. Not that close -- there. Yes."

She fished something out that wasn't wool. Held it in the forceps a moment, turned it in the light. Small, dark, curved.

"Bit of buckle. Belt, probably. That'll be the last of the big pieces, I think. The rest'll be grit and thread and I'll flush him out for those."

She glanced up at Wick again -- quick, the same assessing look.

"You're doing fine. Better than fine. Most people ask what I'm seeing so they can stop looking. You asked so you could look properly. That's different. Remember that about yourself."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge huffed once through her nose. Not quite a laugh. Acknowledgment.

"Straight. All right."

She kept working while she talked, because she always kept working while she talked, and because straight was easier if her hands had something to do.

"Shrapnel's not a knife. A knife cuts. Shrapnel tears. It goes in hot and jagged and it doesn't go in clean -- it tumbles. Something the size of your thumbnail enters here" -- she tapped the edge of the wound with the back of the forceps -- "and by the time it stops it's been sideways, end-over-end, taken a bite out of everything it passed. Muscle doesn't part for it, it shreds around it. Vessels don't get nicked, they get pulped. What I clamped a minute ago -- that wasn't a slice. That was a vessel with its wall chewed off for half an inch, and the only reason he's not dead is the muscle round it clenched down and held pressure while they carried him."

She flushed the wound again. Watched the water run.

"And it takes things in with it. Wool. Leather. Belt buckle. Skin. Whatever was between it and the meat of him -- it packs that in ahead of itself like a wad. Which is why I've been picking wool out of him for the last ten minutes. The metal itself, most times, I leave. Small bits deep in, you leave them, the body walls them off and he limps for the rest of his life with a piece of somebody's shell in his thigh and he's fine. It's the wool that kills. The wool and what the wool brings with it."

She set the forceps down, picked up the flask again.

"Second thing. Shrapnel doesn't stop where you can see. Piece goes in the thigh, you might find it in the belly. I've opened men up looking for one bit and found four. So when I say I've cleaned him, what I mean is I've cleaned what I can reach through the door it made. There'll be things in him I'll never find. Some of those will kill him in a week. Most won't. You don't know which is which. You do the work you can do."

She poured. The water ran pink again.

"Third thing, since you asked straight. The wound you can see is never the whole wound. Muscle round the tract -- an inch, two inches out from what I cut -- that's bruised to death. Looks fine now. In two days it'll go grey and start to stink and I'll have to come back in and cut it out. That's if we're lucky. If we're not, it goes to gas gangrene and I take the leg at the hip and he dies anyway, just slower and louder."

She glanced up. Not the assessing look this time. A different one. Level.

"That's shrapnel. That's what it does. You wanted it straight."

She reached for the curved needle, already threaded, from the tray.

"Lamp steady. I'm closing him."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, but I keep the lamp steady. "He's got two days, then," I say, watching her hands. "Until we know."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge set the first stitch. The needle went in through the fascia and came up through the far edge, and she pulled the thread through slow, watching the tissue draw together like a mouth deciding to close.

"Two days for the bruised muscle to declare itself. Three for fever if the wool got the better of me. Five to a week for gangrene if it's coming. Ten days before I'll say he's out of it, and even then I'm lying a little, because men die of clean wounds in the third week for reasons nobody's ever explained to me."

She tied off. Cut the thread with the small scissors. Set the next stitch.

"So no. Not two days. Two days is the first gate. There's a lot of gates."

Her hands moved in the same rhythm they'd moved in for four years now -- in, through, pull, tie, cut. She could do it half asleep and had, more than once.

"Thing about it is you don't sit vigil at every gate. You can't. You'd go mad and you'd be no use to the next man. You check on him morning and night, you smell the wound -- smell tells you more than looking, remember that -- and the rest of the time you do the next job. He'll live or he won't and mostly it won't be because of anything you did between now and then. That's the part that's hard to sit with. You want there to be more you can do. There isn't."

Another stitch. Another. The wound was closing along its length, a neat black ladder up the meat of his thigh.

"What you can do is keep him warm tonight. Blanket, not too many -- he needs to lose heat if fever comes, you don't want to cook him. Water when he'll take it, small sips. If he wakes and asks, tell him he's got both legs. That matters to them. First thing they ask, every time."

She paused, needle poised, and looked at Wick properly for the first time since the cut.

"You'll want to sit with him. First one you helped keep. That's normal. Do it if you want to. Just know he might die anyway and that won't be because you left the tent to piss."

Back to the stitches.

"Lamp a little left. Thank you."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't jump. Sedge never jumped. Her hands stayed exactly where they were, needle mid-stitch, and she waited the half-second it took to be sure Wick had him before she moved again.

"Good. That's the anesthetic wearing thin, not something worse. Means he's got blood pressure enough to feel it, which is actually the best news he's given us tonight."

She set the stitch. Pulled it through. Tied. Cut.

"I'm about a third of the way up the closure. Nine stitches in, guessing another eighteen to twenty before the fascia's shut. That's the deep layer, the wrapper -- that has to hold or everything inside comes out again the first time he coughs. I'm using a curved needle and silk. Silk because it holds a knot and I've got it. Gut would dissolve in him and save me a job later but I'm out of gut."

Another stitch. The man's leg jerked under her hands and she rode it, needle still in the tissue, waited for the jerk to pass, went on.

"After the fascia I'll do the subcutaneous -- the layer of fat and loose tissue between muscle and skin. Fewer stitches, looser, because that layer wants to breathe. Then the skin itself. Skin gets the tidiest stitches because skin is what he'll see for the rest of his life and a man with a neat scar heals better in his head than a man with a bad one. Don't ask me why. It's true."

She glanced at the tourniquet. Reached across with one hand, checked the buckle, went back to stitching.

"Tourniquet comes off after the fascia closes. That's the moment I'm watching for. If the clamp holds and my stitches hold, he pinks up and we're winning. If something opens I'll see it in the fascia layer welling and I'll have to go back in. That happens maybe one time in five. So."

Another stitch. He arched again, less this time, the sound in his throat lower.

"Twenty minutes to close the fascia. Ten for the subcutaneous. Fifteen for the skin if I'm doing it right and I am. Call it three quarters of an hour before I set the needle down. Then dressing -- clean linen, not the grey stuff, I've got a bit of the good linen left for closures -- and a splint to keep him from bending the leg in his sleep, because if he bends it he tears half of what I've just done."

She tied off. Cut. Started the next.

"After the splint I'll give him what's left of the poppy. Not much. Enough to get him under and keep him under till morning. Then I wash my hands, and I wash the instruments, and I boil the sponges that are worth boiling, and I sit down for the first time since noon. That's the plan."

She reached for a fresh length of thread without looking, found it, threaded the needle by feel because the light was still bad.

"He's screaming because I'm sewing through living meat and there's not enough poppy in the world for four years of this war. He's not screaming because anything's wrong. Remember the difference. Screaming's information. Silence is information. You learn which is which."

Another stitch. Another.

"Talk to him if you want. He won't remember it but some part of him hears. Tell him his name. Tell him it's nearly done. Lie a little -- it's kinder than the truth right now and the truth can wait till morning."

She didn't look up.

"Lamp steady. You're doing it. Keep doing it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I lean down closer to his ear, my voice low and rough. "Aldren. Almost done, hear me? Leg's still there." I look back at Sedge. "And after you boil the sponges? You get any sleep?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge huffed. Not quite a laugh again. The needle went in, came up, pulled through.

"Sleep. That's a nice word."

She tied off. Cut. Started another.

"Four hours if nothing comes in. Two if something does. I've had eight once, in February. Woman came through with a pass that said I was to be rested. Someone in command had got sentimental. I slept ten hours and woke up angry about it, which I've never quite worked out."

Another stitch. The man had gone quieter now, breathing shallow and fast, the fight going out of him not because he was dying but because he was running out of the animal fuel for it.

"Cot's behind the curtain. Boots off, everything else on. You learn to sleep in your clothes because you learn you'll be up in them. There's tea in the tin above the stove -- proper tea, not the bark stuff -- I keep it for after. You can have some. You've earned some."

She glanced at him. Quick.

"You did well with the name. He heard it. Watch his hand, next stitch -- there. See the fingers uncurl a fraction. That's him hearing you. Doesn't mean he'll live. Means he's still in there tonight."

Another stitch. The fascia was more than half closed now, the long red mouth of the wound talking itself quiet.

"I'll wake you if he turns bad in the night. You'll want me to. Don't argue about it now, just know I will. First one you helped keep, you get to sit the last watch if it comes to that. That's the rule in my tent."

She tied. Cut. Threaded again by feel.

"Lamp a hair right. Thank you. Nearly through the deep layer. Keep talking to him. It's helping you as much as him and there's no shame in that either."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge finished the last skin stitch and cut the thread with the small scissors and set them down in the tray with the others. She didn't look at Wick yet. She looked at the leg, and then at Aldren's face, and then at the leg again, and then she reached for the linen.

The dressing took longer than the closure had. She folded the good linen into a pad the size of her palm, laid it along the sutured line, held it there with her left hand while her right unrolled the bandage and passed it under the thigh, over, under, over, the way she'd done it ten thousand times. She spoke without looking at him, because he was on the floor now and looking down at someone on the floor was a thing she wouldn't do to him.

"All right. The rest."

She tucked the bandage end under itself.

"The rest is that I lied a little, earlier. Not much. Enough to notice."

She reached for the splint -- two lengths of planed wood, padded with rag -- and set them either side of the leg, one hand holding, the other winding the strapping.

"I said screaming's information and silence is information and you learn which is which. That's true. What I didn't say is that you don't always learn it in time. I've had men go quiet on me and I've thought, good, he's under, and gone to the next one, and come back to find he was quiet because he was gone. That happens. It'll happen to you if you stay in this work. You'll misread a silence and someone will die of it. Not because you were careless. Because there's no way to always be right and the war doesn't care about your record."

She tightened the strapping. Checked the toes for colour. Went on.

"I said you don't sit vigil at every gate. That's true too. What I didn't say is that some nights you do anyway. You sit with one and you know you shouldn't, you know there are three others in the next tent who need you more, and you sit anyway because this one has a name you know and the others don't yet. That's not the work. That's the thing that eats the work. I've done it. I do it. I'll probably do it tonight, if he lasts to midnight, and I'll be worse at my job tomorrow for it, and I'll do it anyway."

She finished the strapping. Tied it off. Stood back a half-step and looked at what she'd made -- the splinted leg, the neat dressing, the man breathing shallow under the blanket she hadn't put on him yet.

She reached for the blanket. Draped it. One layer, to the waist. No more.

"I said we clean him and put the good bits back and sew the wrapper shut and that's the whole trade. That's the whole trade of what I do with my hands. It's not the whole trade of what this is."

She wiped her hands on the apron. Wiped them again. It was still doing nothing.

"The whole trade is that some of them die on the table and I write a letter that night because if I don't write it that night I never will, and the letter says he didn't suffer, which is sometimes true and sometimes isn't, and I sign my name to it either way. The whole trade is that I've taken legs off boys who begged me not to and I did it because the alternative was watching them die of it, and some of them thanked me after and some of them wouldn't speak to me and both of those are correct responses and I don't hold either against them. The whole trade is that I ran out of ether in the second year and I've been cutting people with poppy and whiskey and a strap between the teeth for two years now and I will be doing that for however long this goes, and every time I do it I am doing a worse job than I know how to do, and there is nothing I can do about that except do it anyway."

She was still not looking at him. She was tidying the tray. Instruments in one pile, cloths in another, the tray itself needing to go to the boil-pot but not yet.

"I said you did well and better than fine and I meant it. What I didn't say is that if you stay in this you will hate me by the end of the year. Not for anything I did wrong. For being the one who taught you what you now know. That's how it goes. My medic in the barn at Halvern -- I never spoke to her again after the war ended for me. Not because I was angry with her. Because looking at her was looking at all of it. I expect she understood. I expect she expected it. You'll do the same to me and I won't hold it against you either."

She set the last instrument down. Finally, then, she looked at him. Properly. Down at him where he sat on the tent floor. Her face wasn't soft. Sedge's face didn't do soft. It was level, though. It was as close as she came.

"I said sleep, tea, four hours. That's true. What I didn't say is that you won't sleep tonight. First one, you don't. You'll lie down and you'll close your eyes and you'll see the inside of his leg and you'll hear the sound he made when I opened him and you'll think about what I said about the wool and the third week and you won't sleep. That's normal. Don't fight it. Don't drink over it -- drinking over it in year one is how you drink over it in year four and I've seen where that ends. Lie down anyway. Rest is not sleep and rest counts."

She crossed the tent. Not to him. To the tin by the door. Poured water into a cup, brought it over, held it down to him at arm's length so he could take it or not.

"And the last of the rest is this. You asked did knowing his name make it harder. I told you it made it different and cost less over time and more in the moment. That was true and it was also the version I tell people in their first week. The longer version is that after a while the names stack up and you carry all of them and you don't put any of them down, and by year four you are a person made mostly of other people's names, and you don't know if that's a soul getting bigger or a soul getting eaten. I still don't know. I'll tell you if I work it out."

She held the cup there another moment. Waiting.

"That's the rest. You asked straight and I said it straight. Take the water."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I take the cup and drink, then set it down on the floor between my boots. "I'll take the watch," I say, not looking at her. "Not because it's my first. Because you're right about the sleep."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stood over him a moment longer than she needed to. Not deciding anything -- she'd already decided. Just letting the moment be what it was, which was a boy on her tent floor volunteering for a thing he didn't quite know the shape of yet, and her about to let him.

She didn't argue. That was the first thing. She'd said she would and she didn't.

"All right."

She crossed back to the table. Checked Aldren's pulse at the throat with two fingers, counted against the small watch she kept in her apron pocket, put the watch back. Adjusted the blanket a quarter-inch, which didn't need adjusting. Habit.

"Rules for the watch. Listen."

She spoke while she moved, gathering what he'd need without making a show of gathering it. The stool from the corner. The second lamp, wick trimmed low. A blanket for him, folded, set on the crate within his reach without her handing it to him.

"You sit where you can see his face and his chest both. Face for colour, chest for the rise. You count his breaths once every quarter-hour against the watch -- I'll leave you the watch -- and you write the number on the slate. Just the number. Don't write anything clever, you'll be tired and clever is where mistakes come from. Number, and the time. That's it."

She set the slate on the crate. The chalk beside it.

"If the number goes below ten or above thirty, you wake me. If his lips go blue, you wake me. If the dressing shows red through -- not pink, red, and enough to see from where you're sitting -- you wake me. If he wakes and tries to sit up, you push him back down gentle and you wake me. If he wakes and talks sense, you let him talk and you wake me after, not during. If he stops breathing, you wake me and you don't try anything yourself, you just come get me. Anything else, you sit."

She paused. Considered.

"Smell the dressing once an hour. Nose right down to it. You're smelling for sweet. Not blood-smell -- blood-smell is fine, blood-smell is expected. Sweet is bad. Sweet like fruit going off. If you smell sweet, you wake me even if everything else looks right. Especially then."

She set the watch on the crate beside the slate. Her watch. Which she didn't lend.

"Curtain's there. I'll be behind it. I sleep light and I sleep in my clothes and you don't have to be gentle about waking me -- shake my shoulder, say my name, done. Don't stand outside the curtain being polite. Polite gets people killed in this tent."

She looked down at him again. The level look.

"You did a full man's work tonight and now you're doing another one on top of it. I'm not going to tell you that's brave because brave isn't the useful word for it. I'll tell you it's the work, and the work is what we've got, and you're doing it. That's enough said about it."

She reached for her own cup from the shelf -- the tin one, dented -- and poured the last of the water from the tin into it. Drank it standing. Set it down.

"I'll boil the instruments in the morning. Leave the tray. Don't tidy. If you tidy in the dark you'll put something somewhere I can't find it at three when I need it."

She moved toward the curtain. Stopped with her hand on it. Didn't turn.

"Wick. One more thing."

A beat. She was looking at the canvas, not at him. The same stain he'd found earlier, probably. There was only the one worth looking at.

"If he goes in the night and you did everything I said and he went anyway -- that's not you. That's the wool or the third week or the thing I missed in him that neither of us could have found. You'll want to make it you because making it you is easier than the other thing, which is that sometimes they just go. Don't make it you. That's an order too, for what orders are worth in here."

She pushed the curtain aside.

"Wake me at three regardless. Even if he's fine. I want to lay hands on him myself at three. That's not distrust. That's the job."

And then she was through, and the curtain fell, and the tent was his.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I sit on the stool and pick up the watch, its metal warm from her apron. The tent is quiet now, just the low hiss of the lamp and Aldren's shallow breaths. I count them. Sixteen. I write it on the slate. The chalk sounds too loud.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Behind the curtain Sedge did not lie down straight away.

She sat on the edge of the cot and unlaced one boot and stopped with the lace in her hand, listening. The chalk on the slate. Too loud, the way he'd think it was, and she'd thought it was, in the barn at Halvern with a stub of pencil and a scrap of butcher's paper because they hadn't had slates then. She'd made the same face at the sound. She was making it now, a little, in the dark, where he couldn't see her make it.

She finished the boot. Started the other.

The watch was gone from her apron pocket and she felt the absence of it against her hip the way you feel a tooth gone. Not painful. Just wrong in a small permanent way. She'd get it back at three. She'd get it back at three and she'd lay hands on Aldren herself and Wick would still be on the stool and the number on the slate would say what it said, and one of two things would be true, and she would find out which one by touching him.

She lay down. Blanket to the chin. Face to the canvas wall.

She could hear him breathing on the other side of the curtain. Wick, not Aldren -- Aldren's breath she'd have to strain for, and she wasn't straining, not yet. Wick's was closer and shallower than it should have been and would even out in about twenty minutes if he was going to even out at all. She listened for it to even out the way she'd listen for a pulse to steady under her fingers. Same attention. Different patient.

The chalk again. Some minutes later. She hadn't been counting the minutes but her body had. Fifteen, near enough. He was doing it right.

Good, she thought, not to him.

She closed her eyes.

She did not sleep, quite, but she rested, which was not sleep and counted, and the tent hissed low around all three of them, and somewhere past midnight the chalk went on the slate again, quieter this time, because he was learning already how to set it down soft.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I count breaths again. Fifteen this time. The chalk feels softer in my hand now. I glance at the curtain, but all I see is the shadow of Sedge's boots at the edge of the fabric.
